claims.source: Analysis of a panel of RhIV (nLuc) and corresponding HIV-1 (nLuc) viruses revealed that sensitivity to the CCR5-binding antagonist maraviroc was similar for each HIV-1 envelope in the context of either HIV-1 or RhIV infection (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: Matched RhIV (nLuc) and HIV-1 (nLuc) viruses exhibited similar neutralization properties.
claims.source: In general, matched RhIV (nLuc) and HIV-1 (nLuc) viruses exhibited similar neutralization properties (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: Most RhIV and HIV-1 strains were sensitive to the quaternary epitope targeting PG16 and PG9 antibodies.
claims.source: While most RhIV and HIV-1 strains were sensitive to the quaternary epitope targeting PG16 and PG9 antibodies, the RhIV1054/HIV-11054, RhIVSF162/HIV-1SF162 and RhIV V1/HIV-1V1 virus pairs each shared the property of being resistant to PG9 and PG16 (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: The RhIV1054/HIV-11054, RhIVSF162/HIV-1SF162 and RhIV V1/HIV-1V1 virus pairs each shared the property of being resistant to PG9 and PG16.
claims.source: While most RhIV and HIV-1 strains were sensitive to the quaternary epitope targeting PG16 and PG9 antibodies, the RhIV1054/HIV-11054, RhIVSF162/HIV-1SF162 and RhIV V1/HIV-1V1 virus pairs each shared the property of being resistant to PG9 and PG16 (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: The HIV-1V1 strain exhibited near complete resistance to all bNAbs tested, except 10–1074.
claims.source: The HIV-1V1 strain was unusual in exhibiting near complete resistance to all bNAbs tested, except 10–1074 and this property was preserved in the corresponding RhIVV1 chimeric virus (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The property of near complete resistance to all bNAbs tested, except 10–1074, was preserved in the RhIVV1 chimeric virus.
claims.source: The HIV-1V1 strain was unusual in exhibiting near complete resistance to all bNAbs tested, except 10–1074 and this property was preserved in the corresponding RhIVV1 chimeric virus (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The MPER-targeting bNAb (10E8) neutralized RhIVCH505 but did not neutralize HIV-1CH505.
claims.source: In one example, the MPER-targeting bNAb (10E8) neutralized RhIVCH505 but did not neutralize HIV-1CH505 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Discrepancies in the potencies with which matched HIV-1 (nLuc) and RhIV (nLuc) viruses were neutralized by bNAbs may be the result of the HIV-1 and VSV-G cytoplasmic tails imposing different conformations on the Env ectodomain.
claims.source: These occasional discrepancies may be the result of the HIV-1 and VSV-G cytoplasmic tails imposing different conformations on the Env ectodomain.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a possible explanation for observed discrepancies.

claims.claim: There may be differences in Env spike density, heterogeneity and distribution on RhIV virions as compared to HIV-1 virions.
claims.source: Alternatively there may be differences in Env spike density, heterogeneity and distribution on RhIV virions as compared to HIV-1 virions.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an alternative possible explanation for observed discrepancies.

claims.claim: Transgenic mice were generated that express human CD4 and CCR5 exclusively on murine CD4-positive cells.
claims.source: In parallel, we constructed transgenic mice that express human CD4 and CCR5, exclusively in mouse CD4-positive cells, at levels mimicking those on human CD4+ T-cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the generation of transgenic mice.

claims.claim: Transgenic mice express human CD4 and CCR5 at levels mimicking those on human CD4+ T-cells.
claims.source: In parallel, we constructed transgenic mice that express human CD4 and CCR5, exclusively in mouse CD4-positive cells, at levels mimicking those on human CD4+ T-cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the generation of transgenic mice.

claims.claim: The A1 line mimicked the levels of hCD4 found on human CD4+ T-cells.
claims.source: The A1 line mimicked the levels of hCD4 found on human CD4+ T-cells (Figure 3C) and was used in subsequent experiments unless otherwise indicated.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Levels of CCR5 on the CD4+ cells in the A1 mice were similar to levels of CCR5 on human CD4+ cells.
claims.source: Levels of CCR5 (as indicated by fluorescence intensity) on the CD4+ cells in the A1 mice were also similar to levels of CCR5 on human CD4+ cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the characterization of the A1 mouse line.

claims.claim: ~100% of hCD4+ cells in the blood of A1 mice were CCR5+.
claims.source: However, as expected ~100% of hCD4+ cells in the blood of A1 mice were CCR5+ (Figure 3D), while the fraction of CD4+ T-cells that also express CCR5 is known to vary according to tissue location in humans (see discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: hCD4, like mouse CD4, was expressed exclusively on CD3+ cells, but was absent from the CD8+ cell fraction.
claims.source: FACS analysis revealed that hCD4, like mouse CD4, was expressed exclusively on CD3+ cells, but was absent from the CD8+ cell fraction (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: 100% of mouse CD4+ cells (but no other cells) in A1 mice expressed hCD4 and CCR5 at levels mimicking human CD4+ T-cells.
claims.source: Overall, 100% of mouse CD4+ cells (but no other cells) in A1 mice expressed hCD4 and CCR5 at levels mimicking human CD4+ T-cells (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: VSV is extremely sensitive to type-1 interferon.
claims.source: Because VSV is extremely sensitive to type-1 interferon (Müller et al., 1994), we crossed A1, C18 and B4 mice to C57BL/6 mice lacking the type one interferon receptor gene (Ifnar1), generating A1Ifnar-/-, C18Ifnar-/- and B4Ifnar-/- lines.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Müller et al., 1994).

claims.claim: Infection of A1Ifnar-/- mice with 105 PFU of RhIVCH505 resulted in profound and selective depletion of CD4+ T-cells 4 days later.
claims.source: We first infected A1Ifnar-/- mice with 105 PFU of RhIVCH505 by intraperitoneal injection (i.p.). FACS analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) 4 days later revealed profound and selective depletion of CD4+ T-cells (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Infection of A1Ifnar-/- mice with 105 PFU of RhIVCH505 resulted in progressive and profound reductions in CD4+ T-cell numbers in PBMC and spleen.
claims.source: Next, we infected a cohort of A1Ifnar-/- mice with 105 PFU of RhIVCH505 and measured CD4+ T-cell numbers and viral RNA levels in lymphoid tissues. This analysis revealed progressive and profound reductions in CD4+ T-cell numbers in PBMC and spleen, and near complete depletion of CD4+ T-cells from thymus and lymph nodes (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Infection of A1Ifnar-/- mice with 105 PFU of RhIVCH505 resulted in near complete depletion of CD4+ T-cells from thymus and lymph nodes.
claims.source: Next, we infected a cohort of A1Ifnar-/- mice with 105 PFU of RhIVCH505 and measured CD4+ T-cell numbers and viral RNA levels in lymphoid tissues. This analysis revealed progressive and profound reductions in CD4+ T-cell numbers in PBMC and spleen, and near complete depletion of CD4+ T-cells from thymus and lymph nodes (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Viral RNA levels peaked at between 103 and 106 copies/μg of cellular RNA between day 1 and day 4 after infection, depending on the tissue.
claims.source: Viral RNA levels peaked at between 103 and 106 copies/μg of cellular RNA between day 1 and day 4 after infection, depending on the tissue, with the highest levels (>106 copies/μg) found in thymus (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The highest levels of viral RNA (>106 copies/μg) were found in thymus.
claims.source: Viral RNA levels peaked at between 103 and 106 copies/μg of cellular RNA between day 1 and day 4 after infection, depending on the tissue, with the highest levels (>106 copies/μg) found in thymus (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Plasma viremia peaked at between 106 and 108 RNA copies/ml on day 1 after infection with RhIV strains.
claims.source: Plasma viremia peaked at between 106 and 108 RNA copies/ml on day 1 after infection, then declined rapidly during days 1–7 and was cleared before day 14 (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: Plasma viremia declined rapidly during days 1–7 and was cleared before day 14 after RhIV infection.
claims.source: Plasma viremia peaked at between 106 and 108 RNA copies/ml on day 1 after infection, then declined rapidly during days 1–7 and was cleared before day 14 (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: CD4+ T cells were nearly completely depleted from blood by day 4 after RhIV infection, then gradually recovered.
claims.source: CD4+ T cells were nearly completely depleted from blood by day 4, then gradually recovered (Figure 4C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: Infection of A1Ifnar-/- mice with 103 PFU of RhIV strains established robust infection with profound CD4+ T-cell depletion, albeit with reduced peak plasma viremia (105–107 RNA copies/ml).
claims.source: Infection of A1Ifnar-/- mice with reduced doses of RhIVBG505, RhIVDu156, RhIVSF162, or RhIVCH505 revealed that 103 PFU established robust infection with profound CD4+ T-cell depletion, albeit with reduced peak plasma viremia (105–107 RNA copies/ml, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Infection of immunocompetent (A1Ifnar+/+) mice with 105 PFU of RhIVBG505, RhIVDu156, or RhIVSF162 yielded robust infection albeit with ~10 to 100-fold reduced peak viremia as compared to A1Ifnar-/- mice.
claims.source: Infection of immunocompetent (A1Ifnar+/+) mice with 105 PFU of RhIVBG505, RhIVDu156, or RhIVSF162 yielded robust infection albeit with ~10 to 100-fold reduced peak viremia as compared to A1Ifnar-/- mice, (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: RhIVSF162 appeared to cause more profound CD4+ T-cell depletion than RhIVBG505 and RhIVDu156 in A1Ifnar+/+ mice, despite reaching similar or lower levels of plasma viremia.
claims.source: A1Ifnar+/+ mice also revealed apparent differences in the ability of RhIV strains to cause CD4+ T-cell depletion that did not correlate with differences in plasma viremia. RhIVSF162 appeared to cause more profound CD4+ T-cell depletion than RhIVBG505 and RhIVDu156, despite reaching similar or lower levels of plasma viremia (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The RhIVCH505 strain exhibited exquisite sensitivity to CD4 expression levels.
claims.source: The RhIVCH505 strain, bearing a T/F HIV-1 Env protein, exhibited exquisite sensitivity to CD4 expression levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the sensitivity of RhIVCH505 to CD4 expression levels.

claims.claim: Infection of C18Ifnar-/- mice with RhIVCH505 resulted in 1000-fold lower peak viremia compared to A1Ifnar-/- mice.
claims.source: Infection of C18Ifnar-/- mice resulted in 1000-fold lower peak viremia compared to A1Ifnar-/- mice, while B4Ifnar-/- mice appeared completely resistant to RhIVCH505 infection (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: B4Ifnar-/- mice appeared completely resistant to RhIVCH505 infection.
claims.source: Infection of C18Ifnar-/- mice resulted in 1000-fold lower peak viremia compared to A1Ifnar-/- mice, while B4Ifnar-/- mice appeared completely resistant to RhIVCH505 infection (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The RhIVADA strain was comparatively insensitive to variation in CD4 expression levels.
claims.source: Conversely, the RhIVADA strain that bears a macrophage tropic HIV-1 Env protein was comparatively insensitive to variation in CD4 expression levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the sensitivity of RhIVADA to CD4 expression levels.

claims.claim: Infection of A1Ifnar-/- and C18Ifnar-/- mice with RhIVADA gave approximately equivalent peak viremia.
claims.source: Indeed, infection of A1Ifnar-/- and C18Ifnar-/- mice gave approximately equivalent peak viremia, while infection of B4Ifnar-/- mice gave peak viremia that was reduced only ~10 fold compared to the other mouse lines (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Infection of B4Ifnar-/- mice with RhIVADA gave peak viremia that was reduced only ~10 fold compared to A1Ifnar-/- and C18Ifnar-/- mice.
claims.source: Indeed, infection of A1Ifnar-/- and C18Ifnar-/- mice gave approximately equivalent peak viremia, while infection of B4Ifnar-/- mice gave peak viremia that was reduced only ~10 fold compared to the other mouse lines (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: RhIV infection was apparently cleared in all cases.
claims.source: Although infection of A1Ifnar-/- mice, and in some cases A1Ifnar+/+ mice, led to high level viremia and profound CD4+ T-cell depletion, in all cases RhIV infection was apparently cleared.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the outcome of RhIV infection.

claims.claim: CD4+ T-cells exhibited near complete recovery by approximately 40 to 50 days after initial RhIVCH505 infection in A1Ifnar-/- mice.
claims.source: Long term follow-up of a group of RhIVCH505-infected A1Ifnar-/- mice showed that CD4+ T-cells exhibited near complete recovery by approximately 40 to 50 days after initial infection (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: PG16 and 3BNC117 antibodies appeared to provide sterilizing protection against RhIVBG505 infection in A1Ifnar+/+ mice.
claims.source: Both antibodies appeared to provide sterilizing protection, in that no viral RNA was detected in plasma of antibody-injected mice and no perturbations in CD4+ T-cells were observed (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The highest dose of 3BNC117 (1 mg) gave apparently sterilizing protection against RhIVCH505 infection in A1Ifnar-/- mice.
claims.source: As was the case with RhIVBG505, the highest dose of 3BNC117 gave apparently sterilizing protection against RhIVCH505 infection, with undetectable plasma viremia and no CD4+ cell depletion (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: At 0.5 mg 3BNC117, 2/3 mice exhibited apparently sterile protection against RhIVCH505, while a third had barely detectable viremia and minimal CD4+ T-cell depletion.
claims.source: At 0.5 mg 3BNC117, 2/3 mice exhibited apparently sterile protection, while a third had barely detectable viremia and minimal CD4+ T-cell depletion.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the results of antibody protection experiments.

claims.claim: At lower 3BNC117 doses (50 μg and 100 μg), partial protection was observed against RhIVCH505, with low-level viremia (<103 copies/ml) and clear CD4+ T-cell depletion, that was not as extensive as control animals.
claims.source: At lower 3BNC117 doses (50 μg and 100 μg), partial protection was observed, with low-level viremia (<103 copies/ml) and clear CD4+ T-cell depletion, that was not as extensive as control animals (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Following the second challenge with RhIVSF162, only low-level plasma viremia (~103 RNA copies/ml) was detected, and only in a subset of mice.
claims.source: Following the second challenge, only low-level plasma viremia (~103 RNA copies/ml) was detected, and only in a subset of mice.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the results of rechallenge experiments.

claims.claim: The magnitude of CD4+ T-cell depletion following the second RhIVSF162 infection was reduced compared to the first infection in A1Ifnar-/- mice.
claims.source: The magnitude of CD4+ T-cell depletion following the second infection was reduced compared to the first infection (in A1Ifnar-/- mice) or absent (in A1Ifnar+/+ mice).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the results of rechallenge experiments.

claims.claim: Following a third challenge with RhIVSF162, plasma viremia was undetectable, and only minor perturbations of CD4+T cell numbers were observed.
claims.source: Following a third challenge with RhIVSF162 at 84 days (Expt#2) or 91 days (Expt#1 and Expt#3) after the first infection, plasma viremia was undetectable, and only minor perturbations of CD4+T cell numbers were observed (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Challenge of A1Ifnar+/+ mice with VSVMLV-E, 28 days after infection and clearance of RhIVBG505 resulted in no detectable plasma viremia.
claims.source: Similarly, challenge of A1Ifnar+/+ mice with VSVMLV-E, 28 days after infection and clearance of RhIVBG505 resulted in no detectable plasma viremia (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Protection against RhIV infection, afforded by a prior RhIV infection, did not require an immune response to the HIV-1 envelope protein.
claims.source: Given that MLV-E and HIV-1 Env proteins share no sequence similarity, these experiments suggested that the protection against RhIV infection, afforded by a prior RhIV infection (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) did not require an immune response to the HIV-1 envelope protein.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text as an inference from the VSVMLV-E experiments.

claims.claim: A B-cell mediated immune response was not required for the vaccine effect of a prior RhIV infection on subsequent RhIV challenge.
claims.source: Thus, a B-cell mediated immune response was not required for the vaccine effect of a prior RhIV infection on subsequent RhIV challenge.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text as a conclusion from experiments using B-cell deficient mice.

claims.claim: A1Ifnar-/- mice infected three times with RhIVSF162 elicited antibodies that bound all four of the SOSIP envelope proteins tested.
claims.source: A1Ifnar-/- mice infected three times with RhIVSF162 (subtype B, Expt #3) elicited antibodies that bound all four of the SOSIP envelope proteins, whose titers increased after the second infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: ELISA titers were higher with the B41 (subtype B) and BG505 (subtype A) than with the two subtype C SOSIP proteins in mice infected three times with RhIVSF162.
claims.source: ELISA titers were higher with the B41 (subtype B) and BG505 (subtype A) than with the two subtype C SOSIP proteins (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A), partly reflecting sequence similarity between the infecting RhIV strain and the ELISA antigens.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: The second RhIV infection boosted and apparently broadened the antibody response initiated by the first RhIV infection.
claims.source: However, all four SOSIP proteins were recognized and the second infection (RhIVBG505) boosted and apparently broadened the antibody response initiated by RhIVDu156 infection.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the antibody responses after sequential RhIV infections.

claims.claim: A1Ifnar-/- mice generated higher titers of Env binding antibodies than A1Ifnar+/+ mice.
claims.source: A1Ifnar-/- mice generated higher titers of Env binding antibodies than A1Ifnar+/+ mice, thus any potential deficit in antibody generation that might have resulted from the absence of type-I interferon signals was overwhelmed by the larger antigen load following infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: The second and sometimes the third RhIV challenges with either homologous or heterologous RhIV strains increased titers and broadened ELISA reactivity.
claims.source: The second and sometimes the third RhIV challenges with either homologous or heterologous RhIV strains increased titers and broadened ELISA reactivity (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 5A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 5A,B.

claims.claim: Broadly Env reactive binding antibodies were elicited after three RhIV infections, regardless of the RhIV stains used in the three challenges.
claims.source: In most cases, broadly Env reactive binding antibodies were elicited after three RhIV infections, regardless of the RhIV stains used in the three challenges.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the antibody responses after three RhIV infections.

claims.claim: Mouse sera from RhIV infected mice revealed prominent reactivity with epitope(s) on gp41 as well as gp120.
claims.source: Further analysis of sera from a subset of mice challenged with a variety of RhIV strains (in Exp #5) using commercial antigen-loaded diagnostic reagents (INNO-LIA HIV I/II Score) revealed prominent reactivity with epitope(s) on gp41 as well as gp120 (Figure 6—figure supplement 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6A.

claims.claim: Mouse sera from RhIV infected mice did not contain detectable levels of antibodies that could compete with human bnAbs or sCD4 for binding to the CD4bs, the apex of the Env trimer formed by the V2 loop or a glycosylation dependent epitope in the V3 loop.
claims.source: Notably, however, these mouse sera did not contain detectable levels of antibodies that could compete with human bnAbs or (sCD4) for binding to the CD4bs, the apex of the Env trimer formed by the V2 loop or a glycosylation dependent epitope in the V3 loop (Figure 6—figure supplement 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by competition ELISA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6B.

claims.claim: In mice that had been challenged three times with RhIVSF162, weak neutralization activity was observed against HIV-1SF162, but not against a heterologous strain (HIV-1CH505).
claims.source: In mice that had been challenged three times with RhIVSF162, (Expts #1–3) weak neutralization activity was observed against HIV-1SF162, but not against a heterologous strain (HIV-1CH505) (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: In mice that were sequentially infected three times with RhIVDu156, RhIVBG505 and RhIVSF162, no neutralization was detected against HIV-1Du156, HIV-1BG505 or HIV-1SF162.
claims.source: In mice that were sequentially infected three times with RhIVDu156, RhIVBG505 and RhIVSF162, (Expt #4) no neutralization was detected against HIV-1Du156, HIV-1BG505 or HIV-1SF162 (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Three challenges with RhIVBG505 failed to elicit neutralizing activity against HIV-1BG505.
claims.source: Even three challenges with RhIVBG505 failed to elicit neutralizing activity against HIV-1BG505.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the neutralization results.

claims.claim: RhIV infection elicited high titers of HIV-1 envelope binding antibodies that were primarily non-neutralizing.
claims.source: Overall, RhIV infection elicited high titers of HIV-1 envelope binding antibodies. However, these antibodies were primarily non-neutralizing.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text summarizing the antibody responses to RhIV infection.

claims.claim: Convalescent serum from animals that had been challenged three times with RhIV strains exhibited modest protective efficacy in passive transfer experiments with an RhIVSF162 challenge.
claims.source: Nevertheless, convalescent serum from animals that had been challenged three times with RhIV strains exhibited modest protective efficacy in passive transfer experiments with an RhIVSF162 challenge.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the results of passive transfer experiments.

claims.claim: Protective activity of convalescent sera was evident even in the absence of in vitro neutralizing activity.
claims.source: This protective activity was evident even in the absence of in vitro neutralizing activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing the results of passive transfer experiments.

claims.claim: Reduced peak plasma viremia was observed in mice that had received convalescent serum compared to controls.
claims.source: Reduced peak plasma viremia was observed in mice that had received convalescent serum compared to controls (Figure 7D,E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7D,E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,C.

claims.claim: Upon challenge with 103 PFU RhIVSF162, Expt #4 convalescent serum recipients had lower peak viremia than controls, and three of fourteen mice were completely protected, with no detectable viremia and no depletion of CD4+ T-cells.
claims.source: Indeed, upon challenge with 103 PFU RhIVSF162, Expt #4 convalescent serum recipients had lower peak viremia than controls, and three of fourteen mice were completely protected, with no detectable viremia and no depletion of CD4+ T-cells (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The replication cycle of VSV is more rapid than that of HIV-1, with a single cycle of replication typically requiring 6–8 hr.
claims.source: First, the replication cycle of VSV is more rapid than that of HIV-1, with a single cycle of replication typically requiring 6–8 hr (Cuevas et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Cuevas et al., 2005).

claims.claim: The mice generated herein differ from humans in that 100% of their CD4+T-cells also expressed CCR5, because of the tight linkage of CD4 and CCR5 in the transgene construct.
claims.source: The mice generated herein differ from humans in that 100% of their CD4+T-cells also expressed CCR5, because of the tight linkage of CD4 and CCR5 in the transgene construct.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the text describing a difference between the transgenic mice and humans.

claims.claim: Approximately 5–10% of peripheral blood CD4+ T-cells express CCR5 in humans.
claims.source: In humans, the proportion of CD4+ T-cells that also express CCR5 varies according to tissue source and inflamation; approximately 5–10% of peripheral blood CD4+ T-cells express CCR5, while most gut associated lymphoid tissue and rheumatoid arthritis synovial fluid CD4+ T-cells are CCR5+ (Agace et al., 2000; Qin et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Agace et al., 2000; Qin et al., 1998).

claims.claim: Most gut associated lymphoid tissue and rheumatoid arthritis synovial fluid CD4+ T-cells are CCR5+ in humans.
claims.source: In humans, the proportion of CD4+ T-cells that also express CCR5 varies according to tissue source and inflamation; approximately 5–10% of peripheral blood CD4+ T-cells express CCR5, while most gut associated lymphoid tissue and rheumatoid arthritis synovial fluid CD4+ T-cells are CCR5+ (Agace et al., 2000; Qin et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Agace et al., 2000; Qin et al., 1998).

claims.claim: The elevated frequency with which CCR5 is expressed in blood cells in the transgenic mice may accelerate CD4+ T-cell depletion during RhIV infection.
claims.source: The elevated frequency with which CCR5 is expressed in blood cells in our transgenic mice may accelerate CD4+ T-cell depletion during RhIV infection.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a possible consequence of the elevated CCR5 expression.

claims.claim: HIV-1 has a lower spike density than does VSV.
claims.source: HIV-1 has a lower spike density than does VSV (McSharry et al., 1971; Zhu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (McSharry et al., 1971; Zhu et al., 2006).

claims.claim: The number of envelope proteins on a RhIV particle was greater than that present on an HIV-1 particle but less than that on a VSV particle.
claims.source: While we were unable to precisely determine the spike density on RhIV particles, our semi-quantitative estimates indicated that the number of envelope proteins on a RhIV particle was greater than that present on an HIV-1 particle but less than that on a VSV particle.

results.result: RhIV strains were successfully generated encoding diverse HIV-1 Env proteins from clades A, B, and C, including transmitted founder strains. These viruses displayed appropriate receptor specificity, replicated well in vitro reaching titers of ~10^6 to 10^7 PFU/ml, and exhibited HIV-1 Env-specific properties including syncytia formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C11 collectively demonstrate successful generation and characterization of RhIV strains. Western blot (C8), receptor specificity assays (C9), cytopathic effects (C10), and viral titers (C11) provide converging experimental evidence. The design strategy (C5, C7) is supported by prior work.

results.result: RhIV reporter viruses expressing GFP or nanoluciferase replicated robustly in multiple cell types and enabled visualization and quantification of viral replication dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C15 are supported by microscopy data (Figures 1F, 1G, Video 1) and luciferase assays (Figure 1H) demonstrating functional reporter systems. The data show robust replication in GHOSTR5, MT2/R5, 293T/CD4/CCR5, and TZMbl cells.

results.result: RhIV strains exhibited neutralization properties similar to matched HIV-1 strains, with most strains sensitive to broadly neutralizing antibodies targeting quaternary epitopes (PG9, PG16), though some strain-specific resistance patterns were preserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C22 are supported by comprehensive neutralization data (Figures 1I, 2A, 2B) comparing RhIV and HIV-1 strains against multiple bNAbs. The data demonstrate that RhIV strains generally recapitulate HIV-1 neutralization properties, with occasional discrepancies noted.

results.result: Discrepancies in neutralization between RhIV and HIV-1 may result from differences in Env conformation imposed by cytoplasmic tails or differences in spike density and distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are speculative explanations for observed discrepancies (e.g., C22). While plausible mechanisms are proposed, no direct experimental evidence is provided to test these hypotheses. The claims acknowledge uncertainty with 'may be' language.

results.result: Transgenic mice were generated expressing human CD4 and CCR5 exclusively on murine CD4+ T-cells at levels mimicking human CD4+ T-cells, with the A1 line selected for subsequent experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C31 are supported by FACS data (Figure 3B-E) demonstrating CD4 and CCR5 expression levels, cell-type specificity, and comparison to human cells. The transgene design and characterization are well-documented.

results.result: RhIV infection of A1Ifnar-/- mice resulted in profound, selective CD4+ T-cell depletion in blood and lymphoid tissues, with viral RNA levels peaking at 10^3-10^6 copies/μg cellular RNA, highest in thymus.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 are supported by FACS data (Figure 4A) and viral RNA measurements (Figure 4B) showing tissue-specific CD4+ T-cell depletion and viral replication kinetics. The data demonstrate acute pathology following RhIV infection.

results.result: RhIV infection resulted in acute, resolving viremia with peak plasma viremia of 10^6-10^8 RNA copies/ml on day 1, rapid decline by day 7, clearance by day 14, and CD4+ T-cell recovery by 40-50 days.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40, C50-C51 are supported by longitudinal plasma viremia and CD4+ T-cell measurements (Figures 4C, 4D, 4G). The data demonstrate acute, self-resolving infection with immune recovery, a key feature of the model.

results.result: RhIV infection was dose-dependent and influenced by interferon responses, with 10^3 PFU establishing robust infection in A1Ifnar-/- mice and immunocompetent mice showing 10-100-fold reduced peak viremia.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are supported by dose-response data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and comparison between Ifnar-/- and Ifnar+/+ mice (Figure 4E). The data show dose-dependent infection and the role of type I interferon in controlling viremia.

results.result: RhIV strains exhibited differential sensitivity to CD4 expression levels, with RhIVCH505 (T/F Env) requiring high CD4 levels while RhIVADA (macrophage-tropic Env) was less sensitive to CD4 variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 are supported by infection data across mouse lines with varying CD4 expression (A1, C18, B4) (Figures 4D, 4F). The data demonstrate that RhIV strains recapitulate HIV-1 Env tropism properties related to CD4 usage.

results.result: Broadly neutralizing antibodies (PG16, 3BNC117) provided dose-dependent protection against RhIV infection, with high doses (0.5-1 mg) conferring sterilizing protection and lower doses providing partial protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by antibody protection experiments (Figures 5A, 5B) showing dose-dependent reduction in viremia and CD4+ T-cell depletion. The data demonstrate that the model can assess antibody efficacy in vivo.

results.result: Primary RhIV infection conferred protection against subsequent homologous RhIV challenges, with reduced viremia and CD4+ T-cell depletion after second challenge and near-complete protection after third challenge.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58, C92 are supported by rechallenge experiments (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) showing progressive reduction in viremia and pathology with repeated challenges. The data demonstrate development of protective immunity.

results.result: Protection against RhIV rechallenge was largely Env-independent and did not require B cells, as demonstrated by cross-protection with VSVMLV-E and protection in B-cell deficient mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61, C93 are supported by experiments using VSVMLV-E (Figure 6D) and μMT-/- mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C). The data demonstrate that protective immunity is primarily cell-mediated rather than antibody-mediated.

results.result: RhIV infection elicited broadly reactive Env-binding antibodies that increased in titer and breadth with sequential infections, with prominent reactivity to gp41 and gp120 epitopes.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 are supported by ELISA data (Figure 6—figure supplements 3-5) and INNO-LIA assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 6A) showing antibody responses to multiple SOSIP proteins and HIV-1 Env epitopes across different infection regimens.

results.result: Mouse sera from RhIV-infected mice lacked detectable antibodies competing with bNAbs for binding to CD4bs, V2 apex, or V3 glycan epitopes.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by competition ELISA data (Figure 6—figure supplement 6B) showing no competition between mouse IgG and human bNAbs. This indicates that mice did not generate antibodies targeting key neutralizing epitopes.

results.result: RhIV infection elicited high-titer Env-binding antibodies that were primarily non-neutralizing, with only weak, strain-specific neutralization observed against the easy-to-neutralize HIV-1SF162 strain.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73, C88-C89 are supported by neutralization assays (Figures 7A-C) showing minimal neutralizing activity despite robust binding antibody responses. The data demonstrate a key limitation of the model in eliciting neutralizing antibodies.

results.result: Convalescent sera from RhIV-infected mice provided modest protection in passive transfer experiments, with reduced peak viremia and occasional sterilizing protection, likely mediated by effector-dependent antibody activities rather than neutralization.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77, C95, C102 are supported by passive transfer experiments (Figures 7D-F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) showing dose-dependent protection despite lack of neutralizing activity. Statistical significance is demonstrated for some but not all experiments (Figure 7D-F).

results.result: Semi-quantitative estimates indicated that RhIV particles had intermediate spike density between HIV-1 (lower) and VSV (higher).
results.evaluation: Claim C84 acknowledges inability to precisely determine spike density and relies on semi-quantitative estimates. No detailed methodology or data are provided to support the quantitative comparison, making this claim uncertain.

results.result: RhIV strains recapitulated key HIV-1 Env properties including CD4 usage requirements and neutralization sensitivity, demonstrating that the model preserves critical Env-receptor interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 are supported by data showing CD4-dependent tropism (Figures 4D, 4F) and neutralization properties (Figures 2A-B). The claims are also supported by citations to prior work on HIV-1 Env properties.

results.result: Broadly neutralizing antibodies readily conferred sterilizing protection against RhIV challenge with representative HIV-1 Env strains (RhIVCH505, RhIVBG505).
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is supported by antibody protection data (Figures 5A-B) showing complete protection with high doses of bNAbs. This demonstrates the utility of the model for testing antibody-mediated protection.

results.result: The RhIV model enables convenient in vivo study of HIV-1 Env-receptor interactions, antibody activity, and humoral responses in a genetically manipulatable host, recapitulating acute HIV-1 infection features.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 summarize the overall utility of the model, which is supported by the collective data demonstrating Env-dependent infection, CD4+ T-cell depletion, acute resolving viremia, antibody responses, and antibody-mediated protection.

results.result: Several potential caveats and mechanisms are proposed including perturbation of Env structure by VSV-G tail, accelerated CD4+ T-cell depletion due to universal CCR5 expression, and enhanced non-neutralizing antibody effects due to absence of HIV-1 accessory genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C82, C97-C98 are speculative statements about potential mechanisms and limitations. While plausible, these claims are not directly tested experimentally and are presented as possibilities rather than demonstrated facts.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about HIV-1, VSV, and immune responses are cited from prior literature to provide context for the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C32, C78, C80-C81, C83, C90-C91 are supported by citations to published literature. These claims establish the scientific rationale and context for developing the RhIV model.

results.result: The transgenic mice differ from humans in that 100% of CD4+ T-cells express CCR5 due to tight linkage in the transgene construct.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by FACS data (Figure 3D) showing universal CCR5 expression on CD4+ cells and is acknowledged as a known difference from human physiology where CCR5 expression varies by tissue and activation state.

results.result: The findings suggest that protective immunity against a cytopathic, CD4+ T-cell tropic virus can be established without protective antibodies.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 is an inference supported by the demonstration of protection in B-cell deficient mice (C61) and cross-protection with VSVMLV-E (C60). This represents a conceptually important finding about cell-mediated immunity.
